After: a meaning matcher, learned from 40,455 examples of how people actually type each question, opens the answer people mean even when they share no word with it, and keeps shut an answer whose words match but whose meaning does not ("did Jesus have a beard" no longer opens the prophets' strange acts). On 270 never-seen questions read blind, the questions with an answering verse among the first six shown go from 116 to 152, and off verses from 828 to 581.

Every question learns from every example, so words also learn which questions they do not point to. It skips training when nothing changed and fails the build if fewer than 70% of examples find their own question (81% do).
- `route.ts` opens a question when the matcher is at least 70% sure, and shuts a word match the matcher finds under 5% likely. `gather.ts` always lets the matcher's three closest answers weigh in, which answered the most blind questions. `words.ts` keeps "made" and "fire" from reading as "mad" and "fired".

So "pills", "quitting" and "witch" are never read as "piles", "quoting" and "watch". A named book or chapter keeps the verses to it, possessives and large numbers match the BSB, and verses that hold a whole Bible phrase rank first. The help line catches the wider wording above. At Deep, Quotations pairs each Greek word with a Hebrew word it *often* translates in the Septuagint, going by notes in Abbott-Smith's lexicon.

After: Places shades regions in OpenBible.info's own approximate shapes. At Study it lists "What happened here" (Theographic's events, each with its verse), and a switch shows each tribe's land. When the verse is in Joshua 13–19, that tribe's land is drawn by itself. At Deep each event shows Theographic's year, with a note that the years follow one traditional chronology. On desktop the panel now reaches up to the top bar, so the map is about square. In Quotations, 1,625 of the 1,882 word pairs are the Septuagint's own: the Greek Old Testament uses that same Greek word for that Hebrew word in the quoted verse (Matthew 1:23 now pairs παρθένος with עַלְמָה). Pairs that come only from the lexicon are marked "often".

These items come from the follow-up list in #5: a Septuagint–Hebrew alignment, Theographic's Events.csv, a source for regions and the tribes, and a taller desktop panel.

How:
- **Septuagint pairs**: MACULA Hebrew (Biblica, CC BY 4.0) records the Septuagint's Greek word for every Hebrew word. `align::septuagint_words` matches MACULA's words to TAHOT's by consonants, the same way the BSB alignments are matched. Only word positions are published. The file is stored with Git LFS, so `atlas fetch` now downloads such files from GitHub's media server and checks the pointer's SHA-256. MACULA's LICENSE.md lists "Greek equivalents drawn from the Septuagint" under CC BY 4.0. An open issue there (Clear-Bible/macula-hebrew#145) asks whether those equivalents come from CATSS, which is non-commercial. Nobody has answered yet; NOTICE.md records what the license says.

Shapes taken from OpenStreetMap (ODbL), islands and generated circles are left out. For shapes drawn as bands of confidence, the middle band is used. Shading is clipped to land and drawn with a dashed edge.
- **Tribes**: no open dataset has tribal borders. Each tribe's land is drawn around the towns Joshua 13–19 lists for it, using only towns the map is fairly sure of. Joshua 19:47 (Dan's move to Leshem) is left out. The panel says the edges are approximate.

Every Nave's subject (Anger, Prayer, Holy Spirit…) also opens as a list of its verses. At Study every verse found lights up on the map, and at Deep you get the full list and how the verses were found.

The owner's rule for this box is that the Bible is the framework for interpreting the Bible. So nothing here writes or interprets. The build rejects any chain part that isn't word for word in its verse, and any question that names a scholar or a church view.

One exception, for safety: a search about ending one's life or self-harm ("I want to die", "is suicide a sin") gets a single row, "Help, and hope". It shows one line on where to find help today (988, Samaritans, a helpline finder), then whole verses of hope (Psalm 34:18, Elijah under the broom tree, Psalm 42:11, 2 Corinthians 1:8–10, Psalm 40:1–2, Lamentations 3:21–23, Matthew 11:28–29). _Requested by **Shubhanshu** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_011qDT8Q1c7gDodDspnZeS1d?thread=cmsg_011qDT8Q1c7gDodDspnZeS1dBCEyFXgLzTsLBMky6BPXy2)_

Before: the verse you typed often did not appear. If even one word in your search wasn't in the BSB (a King James word like "begotten" or "strengtheneth", a typo like "shepard", or wording from another translation), search showed nothing. When verses did match, they were sorted by how connected they are, not by how closely they match your words, so "the lord is my shepherd" put Zechariah 13:7 first. References with a misspelled book ("Mathew 5:3", "Revelations 21") or written as "John 3 v 16" didn't work at all.

After: the verse whose wording matches comes first. On 117 well-known verses typed from memory, the right verse is now first for 101 of them (before: 71) and in the top three for 113 (before: 80). Misspelled book names and "3 v 16" / "ch 3 verse 16" / "3:16, 18" now open the reference, and the search footer says when a typo was read as a different word ("Read “shepard” as “shepherd”").

**How**
- `crates/atlas-core/src/refs.rs`: if a book name doesn't match exactly, it falls back to the closest book name within one or two typos. This only happens when chapter numbers follow, so "truth" is never read as Ruth. Words like "v", "verse" and "ch" between the numbers are understood, and anything after a comma is dropped. Also added the alias "qoheleth".
- `web/src/data/search.ts`: a verse no longer needs every word. Each verse is scored by how much of the query it covers, with rare words counting more. Each query word also matches its other forms (loved/love), King James wording (thou, shalt, unto, -eth) and small typos. The best 600 verses are then re-ranked by word order, so a verse that has the words side by side and in the same order comes first.
- The build now writes `data/bsb.txt` (the public-domain BSB, one verse per line, about 1.2 MB compressed). The search box loads it the first time it opens. Result previews come from this file too, so a search no longer downloads each book's word-study data. `atlas verify` checks that the file has one line per verse.
- Matched words are highlighted in a softer style, and small words like "the" and "is" are left plain.

Things it still misses are wording differences between translations, for example "the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases", which the BSB words differently. No ESV text is stored or used.

Before: a first visit opened on John 1 with nothing selected and no hint of what an arc is. The study panel used terms like "Hubs", "Min. votes" and a PageRank number, and one verse showed three different link counts. Links that readers voted down were listed and drawn. Clicking an arc opened whatever verse sat under the pointer on the baseline, and on a phone there was no way to clear a selection. The study tabs could shrink to a thin strip, and a shared link to a word study lost the word it was opened from.

After: a first visit opens on Isaiah 53:5 with its arcs lit and Links showing it beside the text. A short welcome card above the reader offers three places to start, each quoting the passage it echoes: Isaiah 53:5 and 1 Peter 2:24 ("By His stripes you are healed"), John 3:14 and the bronze snake, and Genesis 22:8 and John 1:36 ("Look, the Lamb of God!"). "Got it" hides the card for good. A verse shows one count everywhere ("Linked to 37 passages", "39 links ›" on each verse), plus "Among the top 7% most central verses". Vote numbers are explained as net votes, and weak links stay hidden behind a "Show N weak or disputed links" button. On the map, hovering one of the selected verse's arcs lights it and names both ends and the votes; clicking or tapping it goes to the other end. "Show: Strongest / More / All" replaces the slider, a Clear button (and Esc) returns to the plain map, and where book names no longer fit, the run of books is named (Law, History, Prophets, Gospels, Paul's letters). Instructions say Click or Tap to match the device. In the reader, each verse's link count opens its links, the selected verse stays in view as fonts load, and Psalms reads "Psalm 23".

This is Phase 1 of the Layers of Meaning plan. Nothing here changes the data, the Rust engine, or the live site, which deploys only from main.

How: the welcome card is a new `Welcome.tsx` remembered in localStorage (`atlas.welcome`); the first verse is resolved from the atlas directly, so it never overrides a verse the visitor picks while the engine loads. Arc hit-testing in `AtlasMap.tsx` reuses the arc height and sine curve the shader draws, limited to the selected verse's edges, and ignores points where an arc has not yet risen clear of the baseline (wider reach for touch, from the pointer type). `verseEdges` and the new `linkCount` skip edges with zero or fewer votes, so the map, the reader and Links agree. `url.ts` adds `wv` and `wp` for the word-study verse and position. The reader ignores a previous book's text while the next one loads, and its scroll hold is tied to one verse.

Checked locally with a production build under the Pages base path, at 1440×900 and 390×844 (touch): no console errors, tabs at full height, arc hover and click go from Isaiah 53:5 to Genesis 3:15, Clear empties the selection, and a word-study link restores "In Isaiah 53:5". Two independent reviews (bugs, and wording and accuracy) were run and their findings fixed in the second commit.
